title: Capxul Lite on Orthograph
source: a design · how it is meant to work

lines.text: You've built this before. A company's money, on chain. Owners who sign together. Budgets that people can spend on their own. And books that have to agree with all of it.
So you know where the work goes. The same few facts get written again and again. Who may spend. What the limit is. What paid means.
They end up in the contract, the server, the database, the app, the SDK, and now the agent's tools.
An agent can write every one of those in an afternoon. That was never the hard part.
The hard part is the next morning. Is it right? And when one rule changes, what else has to change? To answer, you'd have to read all of it.
Orthograph takes a position on that.
You work on the system: the things in it, who may do what, and what must always be true. That description is the blueprint, and you read it.
Everything below it, the agent writes and the framework makes. And you don't take anyone's word for it. The running system is proved, against stories you agreed to.
So you never read the code to know it's correct. You read the blueprint.
Here's the system we'll build. Call it Capxul Lite.
lines.say: Here's the system we'll build. Call it Capsule Light.

lines.text: A company has a treasury: its money on chain, held by one contract, and controlled by its owners together.
The owners can give someone a budget: so much a month, to spend without asking. That someone can be a person, or an agent.
And every payment lands in the books, with its reason and its receipt.
Notice that things get decided in three places. The chain decides the money. Our server decides the notes and the books. And a wallet decides whether to sign.
Most of the difficulty in a system like this is in the joins between those three.
Start by saying what exists, and where each thing lives.
A store is a file. This one is a chain store, and the contract takes its name from the file: Treasury.
A budget lives in that store. Its holder is an account, and its amounts are money in one token. Every field here is public, because a chain shows everything.
A spend is our note about a payment: who was paid, and why. The reason and the receipt are private, so this thing can't live on a chain. The compiler would refuse it.
That's the first decision the blueprint makes you take out loud: who has the last word on each thing.
Next, how a budget behaves. Active, exhausted, revoked.
Spending has two outcomes: still active, or exhausted. And renewing is a move made by time: every month, from the day it started.
Who may act is a role. The holder is whoever the holder field names. An owner is whoever holds a seat on the treasury.
Roles like these are data, not code. That matters, because they have to mean the same thing in TypeScript and in Solidity.
The same goes for rules. Spent never passes the limit. Say it once, as data, and both sides enforce it.
And there's one more kind of caller: the owners together. Enough of them to reach the treasury's threshold, acting as one.
Now the verbs. Spend, on a budget, lives on the chain. It says what comes in, the move it makes, and who may call it.
There's no route here, and no signature handling. On a chain, the caller is whoever signed.
The other half is ours. Drafting a spend records the reason, on our server.
And here is the join. Draft names what comes next: the payment on chain, with the note's id carried across.
One press of a button is really two operations, decided in two places. Now the blueprint knows that, so everything made from it knows it too.
So what falls out? On the chain side, a contract.
The frame is generated. For each operation it checks the row is there, then the role, then the machine. It runs your handler, checks the rules, and emits the event.
That's the same order the server uses. One enforcer for each operation. Here, the enforcer is the contract.
The only Solidity you write is behaviour: add to what's spent, pay, and say which state it ended in.
And a refusal keeps one name and one code everywhere. Budget exceeded reads the same from the contract, the SDK, the command line and the app.
Now look at it by who's using it.
An owner gets the app, with a grant that collects the other owners' approvals.
A member gets one button: Spend. Her wallet signs, and a relayer sends it, so she never needs gas.
An agent gets the same operation as a tool. It signs with its own key, and the contract holds its limit. That's why you can let it spend.
The accountant gets the books, and every payment's reason. Nothing they do touches the chain.
And anyone at all gets the contract itself: who holds which role, and every event.
You didn't write an SDK for each of them. Each way in is made only for the callers who can use it.

scenes.title: A thing, as you see it

lines.text: For the app, each thing gives you a reference: its state, the fields this caller may see, and the moves open to them right now.
That's your hook, and your headless component. You never declared them. They come from the machine and the roles.
For Ada, the budget offers spend. For Bob, it offers revoke. And when it's exhausted, spend is gone.
Follow one payment through.
Ada says who she's paying and why. A spend is drafted, on our server.
The payment is tried on the chain without being sent. If she's over her limit, it's refused here, for free, before anyone signs.
Her wallet shows the operation's own description, and she signs.
The relayer sends it. The contract checks the role, the machine and the rule, moves the money, and emits budget spent, carrying the note's id.
A follower waits until the chain won't take it back. Only then is the spend paid, and the entry written, in one commit.
Between each of those is a waiting state, and the machine names every one.
Granting a budget works the same way, with one difference. It takes two of the three owners.
You declared that with one word. What falls out is a proposal, an approve button for each owner, and the grant itself, the moment the threshold is met.
How do you know any of this is right? The same way as always: journeys.
A journey runs in a world: a local chain, a local server, and a cast of people with wallets.
Ada drafts, signs, and the treasury pays. Then she goes over her limit: refused, and nothing was sent. Then a month passes on the world's clock, and she can spend again.
A different agent writes these, before the builder starts. The builder climbs until they're green.
And because the machines are data, a check can find holes before anything runs. Here, a spend can sit in sent for ever, if the chain never answers.
Now the question from the start. A rule changes: budgets renew every week, not every month.
You change one line. The model says what that touched: the contract, the client, what's left to spend in the app, the docs, and the journeys that use it.
Everything else is still proven. And you know that without reading any of it.
And it runs somewhere. An environment binds the store to a network, and the server to its host.
One command brings up the contract, the server and the database. One trace follows a payment across all three.
In the portal, you see the system the way you described it: the things, their machines, who may do what, and what's happening right now.
An honest note on where this stands.
The server side runs today: the blueprint, the generated ways in, the handlers, and the proof.
The chain side is decided, and being built: the chain store, accounts, roles on chain, the signed entry, the relayer and the follower.
And four ideas in this film are proposals: the reference to a thing, the next step, owners together, and rules as data.
That's the whole idea. Describe the system once, at the level you think in.
The agent builds below it. The framework keeps every piece in step, and proves it.
And you stay where you should be: deciding how it all fits together.
